title: Copper Isotopes and Calcium Fluoride
topic: Atomic structure, Coulomb’s law, pH, and solubility equilibria

stimulus.content: Figure 1: Mass spectrum of copper: a peak at mass 63 amu with relative abundance 69.2 percent and a peak at mass 65 amu with relative abundance 30.8 percent

prompt: A student studies several metals and their ions. The mass spectrum of a sample of naturally occurring copper is shown in Figure 1.

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 380 250" width="380" height="250" role="img" aria-label="Mass spectrum of copper: a peak at mass 63 amu with relative abundance 69.2 percent and a peak at mass 65 amu with relative abundance 30.8 percent" font-family="inherit" font-size="12" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><text x="190" y="15" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700">Relative abundance (%) versus mass (amu)</text><line x1="46" y1="216" x2="368" y2="216" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".9"/><text x="40" y="220" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor">0</text><line x1="46" y1="170.5" x2="368" y2="170.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".22"/><text x="40" y="174.5" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor">20</text><line x1="46" y1="125" x2="368" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".22"/><text x="40" y="129" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor">40</text><line x1="46" y1="79.5" x2="368" y2="79.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".22"/><text x="40" y="83.5" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor">60</text><line x1="46" y1="34" x2="368" y2="34" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".22"/><text x="40" y="38" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor">80</text><text x="78.2" y="230" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">62</text><text x="142.6" y="230" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">63</text><text x="207" y="230" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">64</text><text x="271.4" y="230" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">65</text><text x="335.8" y="230" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">66</text><rect x="120.06" y="58.57" width="44.08" height="157.43" fill="#ec4899"/><rect x="248.86" y="145.93" width="44.08" height="70.07" fill="#ec4899"/></svg>
figures.alt: Mass spectrum of copper: a peak at mass 63 amu with relative abundance 69.2 percent and a peak at mass 65 amu with relative abundance 30.8 percent
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: The masses of the isotopes are 62.93 amu and 64.93 amu. (i) Calculate the average atomic mass of copper. (ii) How many more neutrons does an atom of copper-65 have than an atom of copper-63?

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 63.55 amu as the abundance-weighted average.
States two more neutrons (same number of protons).

parts.label: B
parts.text: Ion-dipole attractions hold water molecules around dissolved ions. The attraction between water and \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) is stronger than that between water and \(\mathrm{K^{+}}\). Explain this difference in terms of (i) the charges of the ions and (ii) the sizes of the ions.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) has a greater charge than \(\mathrm{K^{+}}\), so the Coulombic attraction to the partial negative oxygen of water is stronger.
commonErrors: refers to electronegativity of the ions
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A 2+ charge attracts the oxygen end of water more strongly than a 1+ charge.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) is smaller than \(\mathrm{K^{+}}\), so water molecules can get closer to its nucleus, strengthening the Coulombic attraction.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Ca²⁺ has a smaller radius, so the distance to water’s oxygen is shorter and the attraction is stronger.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Calculate the pH of a 0.0040 M solution of \(\mathrm{Ca(OH)_{2}}\), which dissociates completely.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates pH = 11.90 using \([\mathrm{OH^-}] = 0.0080\ M\).

parts.label: D
parts.text: The student mixes 40.0 mL of 2.0 × 10⁻³ M \(\mathrm{Ca(NO_{3})_{2}}\) with 60.0 mL of 3.0 × 10⁻³ M \(\mathrm{NaF}\). Calculate the concentration of \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) immediately after mixing, before any reaction.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates \(8.0 \times 10^{-4}\ M\) using the total volume of 100.0 mL.
commonErrors: uses 40.0 mL as the final volume

parts.label: E
parts.text: (i) Write the expression for \(K_{sp}\) of \(\mathrm{CaF_{2}}\). (ii) Calculate the reaction quotient \(Q\) immediately after mixing. (iii) The value of \(K_{sp}\) for \(\mathrm{CaF_{2}}\) is \(3.9 \times 10^{-11}\). Predict whether a precipitate forms and justify your prediction.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{F^-}]^2\).
Calculates \(Q = (8.0\times10^{-4})(1.8\times10^{-3})^2 = 2.6\times10^{-9}\), consistent with part D.
Predicts a precipitate forms because \(Q > K_{sp}\) (consistent with part E (ii)).
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: No precipitate because Q is small.

parts.label: F
parts.text: After the precipitate forms and the system reaches equilibrium, a few drops of concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_{3}}\) are added. Predict whether the mass of solid \(\mathrm{CaF_{2}}\) increases, decreases, or stays the same. Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts the mass decreases, because \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\) (forming the weak acid HF), lowering [F⁻] so Q < Ksp and more solid dissolves.
commonErrors: predicts no change because HNO₃ is unrelated
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Decreases: H⁺ combines with F⁻ to form HF, so [F⁻] falls, Q < Ksp, and more CaF₂ dissolves.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Increases because more ions are added.

sampleResponse: A (i) \(0.692(62.93) + 0.308(64.93) = 63.55\) amu. (ii) Two more neutrons. B (i) \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) has a 2+ charge, larger than the 1+ charge of \(\mathrm{K^{+}}\), so its Coulombic attraction to the partial negative oxygen in water is stronger. (ii) \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) is smaller, so water's oxygen gets closer to it and the attraction is stronger. C \([\mathrm{OH^-}] = 0.0080\ M\), pOH = 2.10, pH = 11.90. D \((2.0\times10^{-3})(40.0/100.0) = 8.0\times10^{-4}\ M\). E (i) \(K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{F^-}]^2\). (ii) \([\mathrm{F^-}] = 1.8\times10^{-3}\ M\), \(Q = (8.0\times10^{-4})(1.8\times10^{-3})^2 = 2.6\times10^{-9}\). (iii) \(Q > K_{sp}\), so a precipitate forms. F Decreases: \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\) to form HF, lowering [F⁻], so \(Q < K_{sp}\) and more \(\mathrm{CaF_{2}}\) dissolves.

title: Lactic Acid
topic: Empirical formulas, acid-base titration, buffers, and kinetics

stimulus.content:
Part B, Figure 1: Titration curve of 25.00 mL lactic acid with 0.1000 M NaOH. The pH starts near 2.5, rises gradually through a buffer region (pH about 3.9 at 9.2 mL), jumps steeply near 18.4 mL, and levels off near pH 12

Part C, Table 1
Trial | [HLac] (M) | [X] (M) | Initial rate (M/s)
1 | 0.050 | 0.020 | 3.2 × 10⁻⁵
2 | 0.100 | 0.020 | 6.4 × 10⁻⁵
3 | 0.050 | 0.040 | 1.28 × 10⁻⁴

prompt: Lactic acid, HLac, is a weak monoprotic acid made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. A 0.4500 g sample of lactic acid is burned completely in excess oxygen, producing 0.6600 g of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) and 0.2700 g of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\).

parts.label: A
parts.text: Determine the empirical formula of lactic acid. (i) Calculate the number of moles of carbon in the sample. (ii) Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen in the sample. (iii) Determine the empirical formula, showing how the mass of oxygen is found.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 0.02997 mol H (two H per \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\)).
Finds the mass of O by difference (0.2397 g, 0.01498 mol) and the empirical formula \(\mathrm{CH_{2}O}\).
commonErrors: assumes all oxygen came from the sample

parts.label: B
parts.text: A 25.00 mL sample of HLac solution is titrated with 0.1000 M \(\mathrm{NaOH}\). The titration curve is shown in Figure 1; the equivalence point is reached after 18.40 mL of \(\mathrm{NaOH}\). (i) Calculate the initial concentration of HLac. (ii) Using the curve, estimate the pKa of lactic acid. (iii) Calculate the ratio [Lac⁻]/[HLac] in a buffer of lactic acid and sodium lactate with pH 4.50, consistent with part B (ii).

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates \(0.07360\ M\).
Reads pKa ≈ 3.86 (accept 3.7–4.0) as the pH at the half-equivalence point (9.20 mL).
commonErrors: reads the pH at the equivalence point

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation to find a ratio of about 4.4 (\(10^{4.50 - 3.86}\)).

figures.alt: Titration curve of 25.00 mL lactic acid with 0.1000 M NaOH. The pH starts near 2.5, rises gradually through a buffer region (pH about 3.9 at 9.2 mL), jumps steeply near 18.4 mL, and levels off near pH 12
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: C
parts.text: Lactic acid reacts with an oxidizing agent X. Initial-rate data at constant temperature are shown in Table 1. (i) Explain how the data show the reaction order with respect to HLac. (ii) The rate law is rate = k[HLac][X]². Calculate the value of k. (iii) Give the units of k.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains first order in HLac: comparing trials 1 and 2, doubling [HLac] with [X] constant doubles the rate.
commonErrors: compares trials where both concentrations change
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Trials 1 and 2: [HLac] doubles, [X] is constant, and the rate doubles, so the reaction is first order in HLac.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The rate increases, so it is first order.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates \(k = 1.6\) using one trial.
Gives units \(M^{-2}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\).

figures.caption: Table 1
figures.alt: Table 1: Trial 1, [HLac] (M) 0.050, [X] (M) 0.020, Initial rate (M/s) 3.2 × 10⁻⁵; Trial 2, [HLac] (M) 0.100, [X] (M) 0.020, Initial rate (M/s) 6.4 × 10⁻⁵; Trial 3, [HLac] (M) 0.050, [X] (M) 0.040, Initial rate (M/s) 1.28 × 10⁻⁴

parts.label: D
parts.text: Lactic acid, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)COOH}\), is very soluble in water. Identify the intermolecular force mainly responsible and explain.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies hydrogen bonding between the −OH (and −COOH) groups of lactic acid and water molecules.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Its −OH and −COOH groups form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

sampleResponse: A (i) \(0.6600 \div 44.01 = 0.01500\) mol C. (ii) \(0.2700 \div 18.02 = 0.01498\) mol \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\), so 0.02997 mol H. (iii) Mass C = 0.1801 g, mass H = 0.0302 g, mass O = 0.4500 − 0.1801 − 0.0302 = 0.2397 g = 0.01498 mol. C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1, so \(\mathrm{CH_{2}O}\). B (i) \(1.840\times10^{-3}\) mol \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) = mol HLac; \(\div 0.02500\) L = 0.07360 M. (ii) At half-equivalence (9.20 mL), pH ≈ 3.86, so pKa ≈ 3.86. (iii) \(\dfrac{[\mathrm{Lac^-}]}{[\mathrm{HLac}]} = 10^{4.50 - 3.86} \approx 4.4\). C (i) In trials 1 and 2, doubling [HLac] at constant [X] doubles the rate: first order. (ii) \(k = \dfrac{3.2\times10^{-5}}{(0.050)(0.020)^2} = 1.6\). (iii) \(M^{-2}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). D Hydrogen bonding between the −OH and −COOH groups and water.

title: Lime, Limestone, and Carbon Dioxide
topic: Bonding, thermodynamics, calorimetry, and gas equilibrium
prompt: Calcium oxide (lime) reacts with carbon dioxide to form calcium carbonate: \(\mathrm{CaO(s)\,+\,CO_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,CaCO_{3}(s)}\), with ΔH° = −178 kJ/mol_rxn.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Draw the complete Lewis electron-dot diagram for \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws O=C=O with two double bonds and two lone pairs on each oxygen (16 valence electrons, no lone pairs on C).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: O–C–O with lone pairs on every atom.

parts.label: B
parts.text: (i) Explain why ΔS° for the reaction is negative. (ii) Is the reaction thermodynamically favorable at all temperatures? Justify your answer in terms of ΔH° and ΔS°.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that a gas is consumed and only a solid is produced, so the products have fewer possible arrangements (microstates); entropy decreases.
commonErrors: says the reaction is exothermic so entropy decreases
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A gas becomes part of a solid, so the dispersal of matter decreases.

rubricPoints.criterion: Answers no: ΔH° < 0 favors the reaction but ΔS° < 0 does not, so ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° is negative only at low temperatures.
commonErrors: says favorable at all temperatures because ΔH is negative
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: No. With ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° < 0, ΔG° becomes positive when T is high enough that −TΔS° outweighs ΔH°.

parts.label: C
parts.text: A student adds 1.12 g of \(\mathrm{CaO}\) to 150.0 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The reaction \(\mathrm{CaO(s)\,+\,H_{2}O(l)\,\longrightarrow\,Ca(OH)_{2}(aq)}\) raises the temperature from 21.40 °C to 23.20 °C. Assume the solution has the specific heat of water, 4.18 J/(g·°C), and a mass of 150.0 g. (i) Calculate the magnitude of q absorbed by the solution, reported with the correct number of significant figures. (ii) Calculate ΔH for the reaction in kJ/mol_rxn.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates \(q = 1.13\) kJ (1130 J) with three significant figures.
Calculates the magnitude 56.5 kJ/mol_rxn using 0.01997 mol CaO.
Gives a negative sign (−56.5 kJ/mol_rxn) because the solution warmed (exothermic).

parts.label: D
parts.text: The experiment is repeated with 0.56 g of \(\mathrm{CaO}\) and 150.0 g of water. Predict whether the temperature increase is greater than, less than, or equal to 1.80 °C. Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts less than: fewer moles react, releasing less thermal energy into the same mass of water.
commonErrors: predicts equal because ΔH is the same
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Less than; half the CaO releases about half the energy into the same water.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Equal; ΔH per mole is the same.

parts.label: E
parts.text: Given \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)\,\longrightarrow\,CaO(s)\,+\,CO_{2}(g)}\) ΔH° = +178 kJ/mol_rxn, ΔH°f of \(\mathrm{CaO(s)}\) = −635 kJ/mol, and ΔH°f of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}\) = −394 kJ/mol, calculate ΔH°f of \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)}\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates −1207 kJ/mol.

parts.label: F
parts.text: At a certain temperature, \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)\,\rightleftharpoons\,CaO(s)\,+\,CO_{2}(g)}\) reaches equilibrium with a \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) partial pressure of 0.220 atm. (i) Calculate Kp. (ii) Predict whether Kp increases, decreases, or stays the same at a higher temperature. Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Gives \(K_p = P_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 0.220\) (solids omitted).
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: \(K_p = \dfrac{0.220}{1}\) times the masses of the solids.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts Kp increases because the decomposition is endothermic, and higher temperature favors the endothermic direction.
commonErrors: says K is unaffected by temperature
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Increases: the forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH° = +178 kJ), so raising T shifts it toward products.

sampleResponse: A O=C=O with two double bonds and two lone pairs on each oxygen. B (i) A gas is converted into a solid, so the products have fewer microstates and entropy decreases. (ii) No. ΔH° < 0 favors the reaction, but ΔS° < 0 does not; at high enough temperature, −TΔS° outweighs ΔH° and ΔG° > 0. C (i) \(q = (150.0)(4.18)(1.80) = 1.13\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}\). (ii) \(1.12 \div 56.08 = 0.01997\) mol; \(\Delta H = -1.13\text{ kJ} \div 0.01997\text{ mol} = -56.5\ \mathrm{kJ/mol_{rxn}}\). D Less than: fewer moles of \(\mathrm{CaO}\) release less energy into the same mass of water. E \(\Delta H^\circ_f = -635 + (-394) - 178 = -1207\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}\). F (i) \(K_p = 0.220\). (ii) Increases, because the decomposition is endothermic.

title: Ammonia: Bonding and Phase Changes
topic: Hybridization, hydrogen bonding, and phase changes
prompt: Ammonia, \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\), melts at 195 K and boils at 240 K at 1 atm. Its molar enthalpy of vaporization is 23.3 kJ/mol.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify the hybridization of the nitrogen atom in \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies \(sp^3\).
commonErrors: identifies sp² because of three bonds

parts.label: B
parts.text: Describe or draw a diagram showing one hydrogen bond between an \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) molecule and an \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) molecule. Identify the two atoms the hydrogen bond connects.

rubricPoints.criterion: Shows a hydrogen bond (dashed line) between the N atom of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) and an H atom of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\), or between the O atom of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) and an H atom of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\).
commonErrors: draws the dashed line to the H on the same molecule
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A dashed line from the lone pair on N to an H atom of a water molecule.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: A dashed line between N and the H it is bonded to.

parts.label: C
parts.text: (i) Propose a temperature, in kelvins, at which \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) is a liquid at 1 atm. (ii) Calculate the energy, in kJ, released when 6.80 g of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}(g)}\) condenses at its boiling point.

rubricPoints.criterion: Proposes a temperature between 196 K and 239 K.
Calculates 9.30 kJ released (0.3993 mol × 23.3 kJ/mol).

sampleResponse: A \(sp^3\). B A dashed line from the nitrogen lone pair of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) to a hydrogen atom of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) (or from the oxygen of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) to an H of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\)). C (i) 220 K. (ii) \(6.80 \div 17.03 = 0.3993\) mol; \(0.3993 \times 23.3 = 9.30\) kJ released.

title: Phosphorus and Arsenic Trichlorides
topic: Molecular geometry, intermolecular forces, and gases
prompt: Phosphorus trichloride, \(\mathrm{PCl_{3}}\), boils at 76 °C. Arsenic trichloride, \(\mathrm{AsCl_{3}}\), boils at 130 °C.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify the molecular geometry of \(\mathrm{PCl_{3}}\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies trigonal pyramidal.

parts.label: B
parts.text: A student claims that \(\mathrm{AsCl_{3}}\) has the higher boiling point because of stronger London dispersion forces. Do you agree? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Agrees: As has more electrons (more occupied shells) than P, so \(\mathrm{AsCl_{3}}\) has a larger, more polarizable electron cloud and stronger London dispersion forces.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Agree. AsCl₃ has more electrons and a larger, more polarizable cloud, so its dispersion forces are stronger.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Which liquid has the higher vapor pressure at 50 °C? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies \(\mathrm{PCl_{3}}\): its weaker intermolecular forces let more molecules escape into the vapor at the same temperature.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: PCl₃, because its weaker attractions let more molecules enter the gas phase.

parts.label: D
parts.text: A 4.00 L flask contains \(\mathrm{PCl_{3}(g)}\) at 0.950 atm and 373 K. Calculate the number of moles of \(\mathrm{PCl_{3}}\) in the flask.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 0.124 mol using PV = nRT.

sampleResponse: A Trigonal pyramidal. B Agree. As has more electrons than P, so \(\mathrm{AsCl_{3}}\) has a larger, more polarizable electron cloud and stronger London dispersion forces. C \(\mathrm{PCl_{3}}\): its weaker intermolecular forces let more molecules escape into the vapor. D \(n = \dfrac{PV}{RT} = \dfrac{(0.950)(4.00)}{(0.08206)(373)} = 0.124\) mol.

title: A Magnesium–Silver Cell
prompt: A galvanic cell has a magnesium electrode in 1.0 M \(\mathrm{Mg(NO_{3})_{2}}\) and a silver electrode in 1.0 M \(\mathrm{AgNO_{3}}\). Standard reduction potentials: \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}\,+\,e^{-}\,\longrightarrow\,Ag}\), E° = +0.80 V; \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}\,+\,2e^{-}\,\longrightarrow\,Mg}\), E° = −2.37 V.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Write the half-reaction that occurs at the anode.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(\mathrm{Mg(s)\,\longrightarrow\,Mg^{2+}(aq)\,+\,2e^{-}}\).
commonErrors: puts electrons on the wrong side

parts.label: B
parts.text: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the overall cell reaction.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(\mathrm{Mg(s)\,+\,2Ag^{+}(aq)\,\longrightarrow\,Mg^{2+}(aq)\,+\,2Ag(s)}\).

parts.label: C
parts.text: As the cell operates, which electrode changes mass by the greater amount? Justify your answer using the stoichiometry of the reaction and molar masses.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the silver electrode: per mole of reaction, 2 mol Ag (215.7 g) are deposited while 1 mol Mg (24.31 g) is consumed.
commonErrors: compares only molar masses without the 2:1 ratio
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Silver: 2 × 107.87 = 215.7 g Ag gained for every 24.31 g Mg lost.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Calculate E° for the cell.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates +3.17 V.
commonErrors: subtracts in the wrong order (−3.17 V)

sampleResponse: A \(\mathrm{Mg(s)\,\longrightarrow\,Mg^{2+}(aq)\,+\,2e^{-}}\). B \(\mathrm{Mg(s)\,+\,2Ag^{+}(aq)\,\longrightarrow\,Mg^{2+}(aq)\,+\,2Ag(s)}\). C The silver electrode: for each mole of reaction, 2 mol Ag (215.7 g) are deposited while only 1 mol Mg (24.31 g) is lost. D E° = 0.80 V − (−2.37 V) = 3.17 V.

title: Hypochlorite and Peroxide
prompt: Household bleach contains the hypochlorite ion, \(\mathrm{OCl^{-}}\), a weak base. A 0.20 M \(\mathrm{NaOCl}\) solution has [OH⁻] = 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ M at 25 °C.

parts.label: A
parts.text: When \(\mathrm{OCl^{-}}\) acts as a base, a proton bonds to one of its atoms. Identify that atom.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the oxygen atom (forming H–O–Cl).

parts.label: B
parts.text: (i) Calculate \(K_b\) for \(\mathrm{OCl^{-}}\). (ii) Calculate \(K_a\) for \(\mathrm{HOCl}\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates \(K_a = \dfrac{1.0\times10^{-14}}{3.4\times10^{-7}} = 2.9\times10^{-8}\), consistent with part B (i).

parts.label: C
parts.text: Iodide ion speeds the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide by this mechanism. Step 1: \(\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}\,+\,I^{-}\,\longrightarrow\,H_{2}O\,+\,IO^{-}}\). Step 2: \(\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}\,+\,IO^{-}\,\longrightarrow\,H_{2}O\,+\,O_{2}\,+\,I^{-}}\). A student claims that \(\mathrm{IO^{-}}\) is a catalyst. Do you agree? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Disagrees: \(\mathrm{IO^{-}}\) is produced in step 1 and consumed in step 2, so it is an intermediate; \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\), consumed then regenerated, is the catalyst.
commonErrors: agrees because IO⁻ is not in the overall equation
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Disagree. IO⁻ forms first and is used up later, so it is an intermediate; I⁻ is the catalyst.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Agree, it does not appear in the overall reaction.

sampleResponse: A The oxygen atom. B (i) \(K_b = \dfrac{(2.6\times10^{-4})^2}{0.20} = 3.4\times10^{-7}\). (ii) \(K_a = \dfrac{1.0\times10^{-14}}{3.4\times10^{-7}} = 2.9\times10^{-8}\). C Disagree: \(\mathrm{IO^{-}}\) is produced in step 1 and consumed in step 2, so it is an intermediate. \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) is consumed in step 1 and regenerated in step 2, so it is the catalyst.

title: Dissolving Magnesium Sulfate
prompt: A student dissolves 3.00 g of anhydrous \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}}\) (molar mass 120.37 g/mol) in 100.0 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises from 22.0 °C to a maximum of 27.1 °C and then slowly falls.

parts.label: A
parts.text: (i) Write the complete ground-state electron configuration of \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\). (ii) Which is larger, a Mg atom or a \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ion? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\) (or [Ne]).
Identifies the Mg atom: its outermost electrons are in the n = 3 shell, farther from the nucleus than the n = 2 electrons of \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\).
commonErrors: says Mg²⁺ is larger because it has a charge
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The Mg atom, because its valence electrons occupy n = 3 while Mg²⁺ has none beyond n = 2.

parts.label: B
parts.text: How can the student tell from the temperature data when dissolution is complete?

rubricPoints.criterion: States that dissolution is complete when the temperature stops rising (reaches its maximum) and begins to fall.
commonErrors: says when the solid is no longer visible only
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: When the temperature reaches its maximum and starts to decrease.

parts.label: C
parts.text: (i) Calculate the magnitude of q absorbed by the solution, reported with the correct number of significant figures. Use a solution mass of 103.0 g and a specific heat of 4.18 J/(g·°C). (ii) Calculate ΔH°soln for \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}}\) in kJ/mol, with the correct sign.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates \(q = 2.2\times10^3\) J (two significant figures, from ΔT = 5.1 °C).
Calculates ΔH°soln = −88 kJ/mol (negative because the solution warmed).

parts.label: D
parts.text: Some thermal energy escaped from the calorimeter during the experiment. Is the magnitude of the calculated ΔH°soln greater than, less than, or equal to the true magnitude? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: States less than: escaping heat makes the measured temperature rise smaller, so q and the calculated |ΔH°soln| are too small.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Less than; the lost heat lowers ΔT and therefore q.

parts.label: E
parts.text: The experiment is repeated with 3.00 g of \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}}\) and 200.0 g of water. Predict whether ΔT is greater than, less than, or equal to the original ΔT. Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts less than: the same amount of energy is released into about twice the mass of solution.
commonErrors: predicts equal because the moles are the same
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Less than; the same q warms twice the mass, so ΔT is about half.

parts.label: F
parts.text: Magnesium fluoride, \(\mathrm{MgF_{2}}\), is only slightly soluble; \(K_{sp} = 5.2\times10^{-11}\). (i) Write the equation for the dissolution equilibrium of \(\mathrm{MgF_{2}}\). (ii) Calculate the molar solubility of \(\mathrm{MgF_{2}}\) in pure water. (iii) Is the molar solubility of \(\mathrm{MgF_{2}}\) in 0.10 M \(\mathrm{NaF}\) greater than, less than, or equal to that in pure water? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(\mathrm{MgF_{2}(s)\,\rightleftharpoons\,Mg^{2+}(aq)\,+\,2F^{-}(aq)}\).
Calculates \(s = 2.4\times10^{-4}\ M\) from \(4s^3 = K_{sp}\).
States less than, because the added \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\) (common ion) shifts the equilibrium toward the solid.
commonErrors: says greater because more ions are present
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Less than; the common ion F⁻ shifts the equilibrium left.

sampleResponse: A (i) \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\). (ii) The Mg atom: its valence electrons are in n = 3, farther from the nucleus than any electrons in \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\). B When the temperature reaches its maximum and begins to fall. C (i) \(q = (103.0)(4.18)(5.1) = 2.2\times10^3\) J. (ii) \(3.00 \div 120.37 = 0.02492\) mol; \(\Delta H^\circ_{soln} = -2.2\text{ kJ} \div 0.02492\text{ mol} = -88\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}\). D Less than: lost heat lowers the measured ΔT and q. E Less than: the same energy warms about twice the mass. F (i) \(\mathrm{MgF_{2}(s)\,\rightleftharpoons\,Mg^{2+}(aq)\,+\,2F^{-}(aq)}\). (ii) \(4s^3 = 5.2\times10^{-11}\), \(s = 2.4\times10^{-4}\ M\). (iii) Less than, because of the common ion \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\).

title: Nitrate, Copper Plating, and N₂O₅
prompt: This question concerns several reactions of nitrogen and copper compounds.

parts.label: A
parts.text: (i) Identify the molecular geometry of the nitrate ion, \(\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}\). (ii) Draw one complete Lewis electron-dot diagram for \(\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies trigonal planar.
Draws N bonded to three O atoms with one double bond and two single bonds, with correct lone pairs (24 valence electrons) and the 1− charge shown.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: One N=O and two N–O, with 2 lone pairs on the double-bonded O and 3 on each single-bonded O; [ ]⁻.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Three N–O single bonds with no charge.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Solutions of \(\mathrm{AgNO_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) are mixed and a white precipitate forms. (i) Write the balanced net ionic equation. (ii) Is this a redox reaction? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)\,+\,Cl^{-}(aq)\,\longrightarrow\,AgCl(s)}\).
Answers no: Ag stays +1 and Cl stays −1, so no oxidation numbers change.
commonErrors: says yes because a solid forms
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: No; the oxidation numbers (+1 for Ag, −1 for Cl) do not change.

parts.label: C
parts.text: For \(\mathrm{Zn(s)\,+\,Cu^{2+}(aq)\,\longrightarrow\,Zn^{2+}(aq)\,+\,Cu(s)}\), E° = +1.10 V. Calculate ΔG° in kJ/mol_rxn and state whether the reaction is thermodynamically favorable under standard conditions.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates \(\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ = -(2)(96{,}485)(1.10) = -212\ \mathrm{kJ/mol_{rxn}}\) and concludes favorable.

parts.label: D
parts.text: A current of 2.50 A passes through a \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}}\) solution for 1800 s, depositing copper on the cathode. Calculate (i) the moles of electrons transferred and (ii) the mass of copper deposited.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 0.0466 mol of electrons.
Calculates 1.48 g Cu using 2 mol e⁻ per mol Cu.
commonErrors: uses 1 mol e⁻ per Cu (2.96 g)

parts.label: E
parts.text: The decomposition of \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{5}}\) was monitored at constant temperature (Table 1). Explain how the data show that the reaction is first order.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains first order: the half-life is constant (about 23 min), or ln[N₂O₅] versus time is linear (equal time intervals give equal concentration ratios, about 0.74).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Each 10-minute interval multiplies the concentration by about 0.74, so ln[N₂O₅] versus t is a straight line.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The concentration goes down over time.

figures.caption: Table 1
figures.alt: Table 1: Time (min) 0, [N₂O₅] (M) 0.0800; Time (min) 10, [N₂O₅] (M) 0.0592; Time (min) 20, [N₂O₅] (M) 0.0438; Time (min) 30, [N₂O₅] (M) 0.0324; Time (min) 40, [N₂O₅] (M) 0.0240

parts.label: F
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant k, including units.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates k ≈ 0.030 min⁻¹ (accept 0.029–0.031).

parts.label: G
parts.text: The experiment is repeated at the same temperature with an initial [N₂O₅] of 0.0400 M. Describe the graph of ln[N₂O₅] versus time for the new experiment compared with the original.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a straight line starting at ln(0.0400) ≈ −3.22 and parallel to (same slope as) the original line, which starts at ln(0.0800) ≈ −2.53.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A parallel line shifted down by ln 2, starting at −3.22.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: A line with half the slope.

sampleResponse: A (i) Trigonal planar. (ii) N in the center with one N=O double bond and two N–O single bonds; the double-bonded O has two lone pairs, each single-bonded O has three; brackets with a 1− charge. B (i) \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)\,+\,Cl^{-}(aq)\,\longrightarrow\,AgCl(s)}\). (ii) No; Ag remains +1 and Cl remains −1. C \(\Delta G^\circ = -(2)(96{,}485)(1.10) = -212\ \mathrm{kJ/mol_{rxn}}\): favorable. D (i) \((2.50)(1800) = 4500\) C; \(4500 \div 96{,}485 = 0.0466\) mol e⁻. (ii) \(0.0233\) mol Cu \(\times 63.55 = 1.48\) g. E The half-life is constant (about 23 min); equal time intervals give the same fractional decrease, so ln[N₂O₅] vs. t is linear. F \(k = \ln(0.0800/0.0240)/40 = 0.030\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\). G A straight line parallel to the original, starting at ln(0.0400) = −3.22 instead of −2.53.

title: Formic Acid

stimulus.content: Part D, Figure 1: Titration curve of 20.00 mL formic acid with 0.125 M NaOH. The pH starts near 2.4, rises through a buffer region, jumps steeply at 16.0 mL, and levels off near pH 12

prompt: Formic acid, \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\), is a weak acid with \(K_a = 1.8\times10^{-4}\) at 25 °C: \(\mathrm{HCOOH(aq)\,+\,H_{2}O(l)\,\rightleftharpoons\,H_{3}O^{+}(aq)\,+\,HCOO^{-}(aq)}\).

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify one conjugate acid-base pair in the equation.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\)/\(\mathrm{HCOO^{-}}\) or \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}\)/\(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\), with the acid and base labeled.

parts.label: B
parts.text: A 0.100 M solution of \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\) has a pH of 2.38. (i) Calculate [H₃O⁺]. (ii) Calculate the equilibrium [HCOOH].

parts.label: C
parts.text: At 50 °C, an equilibrium solution has \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = [\mathrm{HCOO^-}] = 4.4\times10^{-3}\ M\) and [HCOOH] = 0.0956 M. (i) Calculate \(K_a\) at 50 °C. (ii) Is the ionization of formic acid endothermic or exothermic? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Concludes endothermic because Ka increases with temperature (consistent with part C (i)).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Endothermic: K is larger at the higher temperature.

parts.label: D
parts.text: A 20.00 mL sample of \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\) is titrated with 0.125 M \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) (Figure 1). Estimate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubricPoints.criterion: Estimates about 8.2 (accept 7 < pH ≤ 10).
commonErrors: says 7 for a weak acid titration

figures.alt: Titration curve of 20.00 mL formic acid with 0.125 M NaOH. The pH starts near 2.4, rises through a buffer region, jumps steeply at 16.0 mL, and levels off near pH 12
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: E
parts.text: The equivalence point occurs at 16.00 mL. Calculate the initial concentration of the \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\) sample.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 0.100 M.

parts.label: F
parts.text: Identify the volume of \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) at which pH = pKa, and give that pH.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies 8.00 mL (half-equivalence) with pH ≈ 3.74.

parts.label: G
parts.text: Calculate K for the reaction \(\mathrm{HCOOH(aq)\,+\,OH^{-}(aq)\,\longrightarrow\,HCOO^{-}(aq)\,+\,H_{2}O(l)}\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates \(K = \dfrac{K_a}{K_w} = 1.8\times10^{10}\).

parts.label: H
parts.text: A student suggests methyl red (color change pH 4.4–6.2) as the indicator for this titration. Do you agree? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Disagrees: methyl red changes color well before the equivalence point (pH about 8.2); an indicator such as phenolphthalein (8.2–10) is better.
commonErrors: agrees because it changes color during the titration
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Disagree; its range ends far below the equivalence pH of about 8.2, so phenolphthalein is better.

sampleResponse: A \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\) (acid) and \(\mathrm{HCOO^{-}}\) (conjugate base). B (i) \(10^{-2.38} = 4.2\times10^{-3}\ M\). (ii) 0.100 − 0.0042 = 0.096 M. C (i) \(K_a = (4.4\times10^{-3})^2/0.0956 = 2.0\times10^{-4}\). (ii) Endothermic, since \(K_a\) increases at higher temperature. D About 8.2. E \(2.00\times10^{-3}\) mol \(\div 0.02000\) L = 0.100 M. F At 8.00 mL, pH = pKa = 3.74. G \(K = K_a/K_w = 1.8\times10^{10}\). H Disagree: methyl red changes color well before the equivalence point near pH 8.2; phenolphthalein would be better.

title: N₂O₄ and NO₂ Equilibrium
prompt: Dinitrogen tetroxide dissociates: \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g)\,\rightleftharpoons\,2NO_{2}(g)}\). The reaction breaks the N–N single bond in \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\).

parts.label: A
parts.text: Explain why less energy is needed to break the N–N bond in \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\) than the bond in \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) has a triple bond (bond order 3), which is shorter and stronger than the N–N single bond.
commonErrors: says N₂ is a smaller molecule
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: N₂ has a triple bond, which is much stronger than a single bond.

parts.label: B
parts.text: A rigid flask initially contains \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\) at 0.600 atm and no \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\). At equilibrium the partial pressure of \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) is 0.360 atm. (i) Calculate the equilibrium partial pressure of \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\). (ii) Calculate Kp.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 0.420 atm (0.600 − ½ × 0.360).
Calculates Kp = 0.309, consistent with part B (i).

parts.label: C
parts.text: The dissociation is thermodynamically favorable only at high temperatures. A student claims the reaction is endothermic. Do you agree? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Agrees: moles of gas increase, so ΔS° > 0; since ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° is negative only at high T, ΔH° must be positive.
commonErrors: disagrees because breaking bonds releases energy
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Agree. ΔS° > 0 (1 mol gas → 2 mol), and favorability only at high T means ΔH° > 0.

sampleResponse: A \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) has a triple bond, which is shorter and stronger than the N–N single bond in \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\). B (i) \(0.600 - \tfrac{1}{2}(0.360) = 0.420\) atm. (ii) \(K_p = (0.360)^2/0.420 = 0.309\). C Agree: one mole of gas forms two, so ΔS° > 0. Because ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° is negative only at high temperature, ΔH° must be positive (endothermic).

title: Halomethanes
topic: Bond polarity, VSEPR, and intermolecular forces
prompt: Halomethanes are molecules in which halogen atoms replace hydrogen atoms in methane. Carbon tetrachloride, \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\), boils at 77 °C; dichloromethane, \(\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl_{2}}\), boils at 40 °C.

parts.label: A
parts.text: In \(\mathrm{CH_{2}FCl}\), which bond is the most polar? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the C–F bond, because F has the greatest electronegativity difference from C.
commonErrors: picks C–Cl because Cl is larger
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: C–F: the electronegativity difference between C and F is the greatest.

parts.label: B
parts.text: The H–O–H bond angle in water (104.5°) is smaller than the H–C–H angle in methane (109.5°). Explain.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that the two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs do, compressing the angle.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Lone pairs take up more space and push the O–H bonds closer together.

parts.label: C
parts.text: (i) Identify all types of intermolecular forces in liquid \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) and in liquid \(\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl_{2}}\). (ii) Explain why \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) has the higher boiling point.

rubricPoints.criterion: \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\): London dispersion only. \(\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl_{2}}\): London dispersion and dipole-dipole.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: CCl₄: LDF; CH₂Cl₂: LDF and dipole-dipole.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) has more electrons and a larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so its London forces exceed the combined forces in \(\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl_{2}}\).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: CCl₄’s much larger electron cloud gives stronger dispersion forces than CH₂Cl₂’s dispersion plus dipole forces.

sampleResponse: A The C–F bond, since the electronegativity difference between C and F is the largest. B The two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, so the H–O–H angle is compressed below 109.5°. C (i) \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\): London dispersion forces only; \(\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl_{2}}\): London dispersion and dipole-dipole forces. (ii) \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) has more electrons and a larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so its dispersion forces are stronger than the combined forces among \(\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl_{2}}\) molecules.

parts.label: A
parts.text: A particle view of a small volume of one standard solution shows 6 \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ions, and the solution has an absorbance of 0.30. How many \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ions would appear in the same volume of a solution with an absorbance of 0.15? Explain.

rubricPoints.criterion: States 3 ions, because absorbance is directly proportional to concentration.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: 3 ions; half the absorbance means half the concentration.

parts.label: B
parts.text: The diluted unknown has an absorbance of 0.42. (i) Determine its \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) concentration. (ii) The diluted unknown was made by diluting 5.00 mL of the original solution to 50.00 mL. Calculate the concentration of the original solution.

rubricPoints.criterion: Determines 0.035 M (accept 0.034–0.036) from the graph or A = εbc with ε = 12.0 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹.
Calculates 0.35 M using M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, consistent with part B (i).

parts.label: C
parts.text: The cuvette holding the unknown had fingerprints on its outer surface that absorbed some light. A student claims this made the calculated concentration of the original solution too low. Do you agree? Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Disagrees: the fingerprints increase the measured absorbance, which gives a calculated concentration that is too high.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Disagree; extra absorbed light raises A, so the calculated concentration is too high.

sampleResponse: A 3 ions: absorbance is proportional to concentration, so half the absorbance means half as many ions in the same volume. B (i) From the slope, ε = 12.0 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹, so \(c = 0.42/12.0 = 0.035\ M\). (ii) \(M_1 = (0.035)(50.00)/5.00 = 0.35\ M\). C Disagree: the fingerprints raise the measured absorbance, so the calculated concentration is too high.

title: Burning Magnesium
prompt: Magnesium burns in oxygen: \(\mathrm{2Mg(s)\,+\,O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2MgO(s)}\), ΔH° = −1203 kJ/mol_rxn.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Calculate ΔH°f for \(\mathrm{MgO(s)}\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates −602 kJ/mol (half of −1203).

parts.label: B
parts.text: A 4.86 g sample of Mg reacts with 4.00 g of \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\). (i) Identify the limiting reactant, with supporting calculations. (ii) Calculate the energy released, in kJ.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies Mg as limiting: 0.200 mol Mg needs only 0.100 mol \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\), but 0.125 mol is present.
commonErrors: picks O₂ because its mass is smaller
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: 0.200 mol Mg and 0.125 mol O₂; Mg needs 0.100 mol O₂, so Mg is limiting.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 120 kJ released, consistent with the limiting reactant.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: \(0.200\text{ mol Mg} \times \dfrac{1203\text{ kJ}}{2\text{ mol Mg}} = 120\) kJ released.

parts.label: C
parts.text: The melting point of \(\mathrm{MgO}\) (2852 °C) is much higher than that of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) (801 °C). Explain in terms of Coulombic attractions.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) have larger charges (and smaller radii) than \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\), so the Coulombic attractions in the lattice are much stronger.
commonErrors: refers to covalent bonds in MgO
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: MgO’s 2+ and 2− ions, which are also smaller, attract far more strongly than the 1+ and 1− ions in NaCl.

sampleResponse: A −1203 ÷ 2 = −602 kJ/mol. B (i) \(4.86 \div 24.31 = 0.200\) mol Mg needs 0.100 mol \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\); there is \(4.00 \div 32.00 = 0.125\) mol \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\), so Mg is limiting. (ii) \(0.200 \times 1203/2 = 120\) kJ released. C \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) carry twice the charge of \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) and are smaller, so their Coulombic attractions are much stronger, giving MgO a far higher melting point.
